column5: praise of the name; its exaltation
column6: The commentary makes the name itself the object of praise and hears al-aʿlā with the name; this verse commands all creation to praise YHWH’s name because it alone is exalted.

column5: direct-object praise of the name
column6: The commentary stresses that 87:1 acts directly on the name; this psalm tells YHWH’s servants to praise the name itself, not merely to act by it.

column5: proclaiming the name and ascribing greatness
column6: The commentary joins the divine name to height and praise; Moses says he will proclaim YHWH’s name and ascribe greatness to God, a close liturgical formulation.

column5: sanctifying rather than profaning the name
column6: The commentary reads the command as guarding the name from false or unworthy attribution; Leviticus forbids profaning God’s holy name and calls Israel to sanctify it.

column5: name proclaimed through divine attributes
column6: The commentary says the name must not be filled with an unsuitable meaning; here YHWH proclaims the name while describing mercy, grace, patience, and steadfast love, showing the character the name bears.

column5: the high and lofty one whose name is Holy
column6: The commentary preserves both readings of al-aʿlā, highest Lord and highest name; Isaiah calls God high and lofty and says his name is Holy.

column5: God’s name and glory not given to another
column6: The commentary warns against transferring the Lord’s name to rivals; Isaiah identifies YHWH by name and says his glory and praise are not given to idols.

column5: the divine name for all generations
column6: The commentary treats the name as a uniquely guarded designation; God gives Moses the name YHWH as the enduring name remembered through generations.

column5: “Hallowed be your name”
column6: The commentary treats tasbih as declaring God’s name free of defect; Jesus’ prayer asks that the Father’s name be hallowed, making sanctification of the name the prayer’s opening petition.

column5: “Hallowed be your name”
column6: The commentary makes the name itself the focus of the imperative; Luke preserves the same petition in a shorter prayer addressed to the Father, a second early Christian form of the formula.

column5: Kiddush ha-Shem through public conduct
column6: The commentary says praise must become speech, action, and intention; Yoma 86a says Torah-shaped conduct can cause observers to praise God, making sanctification of the Name an ethical public practice.

column5: hallowed name as sanctified in the worshiper
column6: The commentary says God is not made more perfect by tasbih, while the worshiper must speak and act rightly; Tertullian reads “hallowed be thy name” as a request that the already holy name be sanctified in believers.

column5: bowing, kneeling, and worship before the Maker
column6: The commentary brings tasbih together with bodily prayer and prostration; this verse joins worship, bowing, and kneeling before YHWH the Maker in one embodied act.

column5: continual praise as lips confess the name
column6: The commentary says tasbih is both a judgment and a practice carried by speech and body; Hebrews calls for continual praise, the fruit of lips confessing God’s name.

column5: creatures praising without rest, day and night
column6: The commentary distinguishes human tasbih from the praise of creatures people cannot comprehend; Revelation’s four living creatures never stop proclaiming God’s holiness day or night.

column5: elders falling before the throne
column6: The commentary connects divine glory with the bodily place of prostration; Revelation’s elders fall before the enthroned one and cast their crowns down, enacting worship without keeping honor for themselves.

column5: sun, moon, and stars called to praise
column6: The commentary places stars moving in their courses beside created praise; this psalm directly summons sun, moon, and shining stars to praise YHWH.

column5: the name praised from sunrise to sunset
column6: The commentary sets daytime activity beside extended worship; this verse gives the name of YHWH praise from the rising of the sun to its setting.

column5: Hebrew ʿElyon, “Most High”
column6: The commentary labels Arabic al-aʿlā with the ʿ-l-w root; Melchizedek blesses Abram by El Elyon, “God Most High,” creator of heaven and earth, a Hebrew cognate title for the height claim.

column5: Hebrew ʿElyon over all the earth
column6: The commentary joins “highest” to the Lord’s unrivaled rule; the psalm calls YHWH Most High over all the earth and exalted far above all gods, using the Hebrew cognate title in that claim.

column5: no one can be made God’s equal
column6: The commentary hears “namesake” as a rival who could bear God’s name or compete with him; Isaiah asks whom God can be likened or made equal to, directly denying such a counterpart.

column5: YHWH is one
column6: The commentary rejects distributing lordship among separate claimants; Israel’s confession names YHWH as one, the foundational Jewish formulation of undivided allegiance.

column5: “Who is like you, YHWH?”
column6: The commentary connects praise with the claim that God has no namesake; after the sea victory, Moses’ song asks who among the gods is like YHWH and praises his holiness and wonders.

column5: no God beside Israel’s King and Redeemer
column6: The commentary calls rival divine names unsupported names; Isaiah has YHWH declare himself first and last and say there is no God besides him.

column5: many called gods and lords
column6: The commentary describes lordship being distributed among many names; Paul acknowledges many so-called gods and lords in heaven and earth, then sets that language beside the community’s confession in the next verse.

column5: one God and one Lord
column6: The commentary’s warning against separate competing lords meets Paul’s formulation of one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ; the verse also gives Christian readers a distinctive two-part confession.

column5: keeping disciples in the Father’s name
column6: The commentary says the name is to be kept from rival claims; Jesus asks the Father to keep his followers in the name given to him, making the name a sphere of protection and unity.

column5: Jesus makes the Father’s name known
column6: The commentary links a singular messenger, revelation, and the divine name; Jesus says he has made the Father’s name known and will continue to do so, with the result that divine love may dwell in the disciples.

column5: Adam names the animals
column6: The commentary’s Adam scene says God teaches all names and the angels cannot supply them; Genesis instead has God bring animals to Adam to see what he will call them, giving Adam the naming act and a different emphasis on human knowledge.

column5: Hebrew šēm, name sought as renown
column6: The commentary discusses Arabic ism as a name that raises its bearer; Hebrew šēm is its cognate, and Babel’s builders seek to make a šēm for themselves while raising a tower toward heaven, where name and self-exalting ascent meet.

column5: self-made name and tower reaching heaven
column6: The commentary contrasts the true highest Lord with a creature claiming height for itself; Babel’s builders try to make their own name and a tower whose top reaches heaven, an earlier collective version of self-exaltation.

column5: God, rather than the person, makes Abram’s name great
column6: The commentary says a name is raised but its bearer must not seize divine honor; God promises to make Abram’s name great, locating honor in divine gift rather than self-claim.

column5: Aramaic šēm, the name blessed forever
column6: The commentary’s Arabic ism is a Semitic cognate of Aramaic šēm; Daniel blesses the name of God forever and immediately attributes wisdom and might to God, joining name, praise, and divine sovereignty.

column5: Aramaic mĕšabbaḥ, “I praise”
column6: The commentary’s Arabic tasbih is cognate with Biblical Aramaic š-b-ḥ; after God reveals the hidden dream, Daniel says he thanks and praises God, showing praise as acknowledgment of received wisdom.

column5: Aramaic rabbouni, “my teacher”
column6: The commentary hears ownership and care in Arabic rabbika; Mary addresses Jesus with the Aramaic rabbouni, which John glosses as teacher, preserving a related personal master-title in a human address.

column5: YHWH’s name and its proclaimed meaning
column6: The commentary insists that a name must not be filled with a false quality; Exodus has God proclaim the name YHWH together with mercy, grace, patience, and steadfast love, a concrete scriptural account of the name’s character.

column5: sanctifying a profaned name among the nations
column6: The commentary says God’s name must be kept from misrepresentation; Ezekiel says Israel profaned it among nations and God will sanctify his great name before them, adding public reputation and restoration.

column5: prohibition against carrying the name in vain
column6: The commentary’s command protects the divine name from misuse; Exodus forbids bearing YHWH’s name falsely or emptily, a legal boundary around speech about God.

column5: God shepherded Jacob throughout his life
column6: The commentary hears owner, guide, and caregiver together in “your Lord”; Jacob calls God the one who shepherded him all his life, making the relation sustained care rather than bare possession.

column5: YHWH seeks his scattered sheep himself
column6: The commentary develops the Lord as one who keeps together what might disperse; Ezekiel has YHWH personally search for and rescue his sheep, a close shepherding image of active guardianship.

column5: binding the injured and strengthening the weak
column6: The commentary connects lordship with bringing what is cared for toward completion; YHWH’s shepherd promises to heal, strengthen, and seek the lost, specifying repair as part of divine rule.

column5: clouds, rain, and mountain grass
column6: The commentary develops the sequence from sky and first rain to pasture; the psalm says God prepares rain and makes grass grow on the mountains, a direct biblical counterpart to the provision scene.

column5: food given to animals that cry out
column6: The commentary relates the Lord to a shepherd and provider; this verse says God gives food to beasts and young ravens, extending pasture’s growth into care for dependent creatures.

column5: human life like grass
column6: The commentary’s pasture turns from green growth to dark, spent residue; Isaiah compares all flesh to grass, framing the vegetation cycle as a picture of human transience.

column5: grass withers and flowers fall
column6: The commentary stresses that the Lord’s ordering includes the pasture’s decline; Isaiah says grass withers when the breath of YHWH blows, making the same growth-to-loss movement a sign of human frailty.

column5: God’s word endures when grass withers
column6: The commentary sets the high name against fading worldly life; Isaiah contrasts withering grass with the enduring word of God, adding permanence to the transient pasture image.

column5: the lot’s outcome belongs to YHWH
column6: The commentary develops the image of arrows gathered in a bag and lots cast to assign a share; Proverbs says the lot is cast but its decision comes from YHWH, connecting chance-like allocation to divine governance.

column5: lots distinguish the two goats
column6: The commentary mentions lots and measured shares among the Arabic root’s developed images; Leviticus assigns one goat to YHWH and one to Azazel by lot, a ritual use of lots to distribute distinct roles.

column5: Moses as God to Pharaoh, Aaron as his mouth
column6: The commentary recalls Moses’ mission and his request for his brother’s help; Exodus appoints Aaron to speak for Moses and calls Moses God to Pharaoh, giving a close but differently framed account of delegated authority.

column5: Aaron’s staff swallows the magicians’ staffs
column6: The commentary recalls Moses’ fear before Pharaoh’s sign-makers and God’s reassurance; Exodus tells the same contest through staffs becoming serpents and Aaron’s staff swallowing theirs, locating the outcome in a public sign.

column5: Pharaoh asks who YHWH is
column6: The commentary presents Pharaoh as claiming “I am your highest lord”; Exodus instead has Pharaoh challenge Moses by asking who YHWH is and refusing obedience, a related confrontation expressed as denial rather than self-deification.

column5: Pharaoh raised so God’s name may be proclaimed
column6: The commentary opposes Pharaoh’s appropriation of the highest lordship to the true Lord; Exodus says Pharaoh was raised so God’s power and name would be proclaimed throughout the earth, reversing the direction of glory.

column5: the king of Tyre says, “I am a god”
column6: The commentary sets Pharaoh’s self-declared highest lordship against the command to keep God’s name for God; Ezekiel’s king makes the explicit divine claim, and the oracle answers that he is mortal, sharpening the usurpation motif.

column5: a king’s resolve to be like the Most High
column6: The commentary says Pharaoh takes the name and height for himself; Isaiah’s king of Babylon vows to make himself like the Most High, an explicit self-exalting counterpart.

column5: the self-exalting king brought down
column6: The commentary contrasts true height with rulers who rise by tyranny; Isaiah follows the king’s ascent boast by placing him in Sheol, giving the reversal that the boast itself invites.

column5: Nebuchadnezzar boasts of the city he built
column6: The commentary links a ruler’s claim to supreme status with the taking of glory; Nebuchadnezzar credits his power and majesty for Babylon, a concrete royal boast before his humbling.

column5: the humbled king blesses the Most High
column6: The commentary’s central contrast is false self-exaltation versus praise of the true Highest; after his humiliation Nebuchadnezzar blesses and honors the Most High, whose dominion is everlasting.

column5: the lot identifies Jonah on the ship
column6: The commentary recounts Jonah’s flight on a loaded ship and the lot that marks him among the losing group; Jonah’s sailors cast lots to discover whose account brought the storm, a close shared episode with a different stated purpose.

column5: Jonah is thrown into the sea
column6: The commentary says Jonah is swallowed after the ship’s lot; Jonah’s sailors throw him into the sea and the storm ceases, giving the sea episode and its immediate outcome in the biblical telling.

column5: a great fish swallows Jonah
column6: The commentary recounts Jonah swallowed while blameworthy; the Hebrew book says YHWH appoints a great fish to swallow him, sharing the rescue scene while identifying divine agency explicitly.

column5: Jonah cries from inside the fish and is heard
column6: The commentary quotes Jonah’s confession in darkness and says God answers him; Jonah’s prayer from the fish says his cry reached YHWH, while its surrounding prayer does not use the same confession formula.

column5: thanksgiving and vowed sacrifice precede release
column6: The commentary says prior tasbih keeps Jonah from remaining in the fish until resurrection; Jonah’s prayer promises thanksgiving and sacrifice, after which release follows, sharing piety and rescue but giving a different causal frame.

column5: the fish releases Jonah onto dry land
column6: The commentary’s fish episode ends with rescue from the belly; Jonah’s book says the fish vomits him onto dry land at God’s command, a direct narrative parallel.

column5: Jonah’s three days become a sign of resurrection
column6: The commentary contrasts Jonah’s deliverance from the fish with remaining there until the day of resurrection; Jesus interprets Jonah’s three days in the fish as a sign for the Son of Man’s time in the earth, adding a Christian resurrection reading.

column5: alms given secretly and repaid by the Father
column6: The commentary cites giving wealth to seek the highest Lord’s face without repaying a favor; Jesus says hidden almsgiving is seen and repaid by the Father, a concrete ethical parallel with divine rather than human recompense.

column5: treasure stored in heaven rather than on earth
column6: The commentary contrasts the low, passing worldly life with what is higher and lasting; Jesus tells disciples to store treasure in heaven, where it is not lost, giving the ethical form of that vertical contrast.

column5: Jesus is called Son of the Most High
column6: The commentary rejects rivals taking the highest Lord’s name; the annunciation names Jesus Son of the Most High and promises him David’s throne, presenting a Christian claim that joins filial language to the highest title.

column5: God gives his only Son
column6: The commentary’s tasbih verses reject the claim that God has a child; John says God gave his only Son, a central Christian assertion that makes the theological difference explicit.

column5: Thomas calls the risen Jesus “my Lord and my God”
column6: The commentary cites Jesus’ denial of a rightful claim to divinity; Thomas addresses the risen Jesus with divine titles, an explicit Christian narrative counterclaim about Jesus’ status.

column5: the name above every name bestowed on Jesus
column6: The commentary says the highest name belongs to God and must not be seized by a creature; Philippians says God highly exalts Jesus and grants him the name above every name, the central Christian reapplication of the exalted-name language.

column5: every knee bows at Jesus’ name
column6: The commentary joins praise to bodily prostration; Philippians says every knee bows at Jesus’ name, extending worship to the Christian confession of Jesus.

column5: every tongue confesses Jesus Christ as Lord
column6: The commentary resists transferring divine lordship to others; Philippians makes universal confession of Jesus as Lord the outcome of God’s exaltation, a distinctive Christian reading of the title.

column5: a mark distinguishes those spared judgment
column6: The commentary presents the alternate Arabic root for name as a bodily brand identifying an owner; Ezekiel marks the foreheads of those who grieve over injustice so they are distinguished during judgment, a motif parallel without claiming Hebrew cognacy.

column5: the Lamb’s and Father’s names on foreheads
column6: The commentary describes a mark as an identifying trace that separates one bearer from others; Revelation’s redeemed bear the Lamb’s name and the Father’s name on their foreheads, making identity and allegiance bodily visible.

column5: the beast’s name linked to its mark and economic allegiance
column6: The commentary warns against a name being assigned to a false claimant; Revelation connects the beast’s name or number with its mark and the ability to buy or sell, a contrary mark of allegiance.

column4: Prayer of Azariah and Song of the Three Young Men 35
column5: all the works bless and exalt the Lord
column6: The commentary distinguishes human praise from the praise of the heavens and creatures; the Three Young Men summon all the Lord’s works to bless and exalt him forever, a liturgical expansion of creation-wide tasbih.

column5: name exalted above all blessing and praise
column6: The commentary keeps the name itself as the object to be raised; Nehemiah’s public prayer blesses God’s glorious name, exalted above blessing and praise, an unusually close liturgical formulation.

column5: no one like YHWH, whose name is great in might
column6: The commentary joins the highest title to the absence of any namesake or rival; Jeremiah says there is none like YHWH and that his name is great in might, joining uniqueness, name, and power.

column5: glory due to the name
column6: The commentary distinguishes praising the name itself from acting by means of it; this psalm tells worshipers to ascribe to YHWH the glory due his name and to bring an offering.

column5: worship in holy splendor
column6: The commentary makes tasbih an enacted practice as well as a judgment; the next line of the psalm calls the earth to bow before YHWH in holy splendor, joining name-praise to bodily worship.

column5: praising the great and awesome name
column6: The commentary says the name is to be guarded and held high; this psalm commands praise of YHWH’s great and awesome name and immediately calls him holy.

column5: the name great among nations with pure offerings
column6: The commentary asks that the name be kept from false attribution; Malachi says YHWH’s name is great among the nations and associates it with pure offerings from sunrise to sunset, extending the name’s honor beyond one people.

column5: the Lord enthroned high and lifted up
column6: The commentary preserves the reading of al-aʿlā as the Lord himself being highest; Isaiah’s vision places the Lord on a high and lofty throne as a prophet receives a commission.

column5: the thrice-holy proclamation
column6: The commentary presents tasbih as declaring God free of defect; the seraphim call one to another “Holy, holy, holy” and fill the scene with God’s glory, a foundational Jewish liturgical formula of divine holiness.

column5: morning stars singing at creation
column6: The commentary notes stars moving in their courses alongside the praise of creation; Job’s creation scene pictures morning stars singing together, making celestial praise explicit.

column5: do not invoke the names of other gods
column6: The commentary warns against assigning divine naming to rivals; Exodus tells Israel not even to mention the names of other gods, a concrete discipline of exclusive worship.

column5: Moses says he is slow of speech
column6: The commentary recalls Moses asking God to open his chest and make his mission easy; Exodus has Moses object that he is not eloquent and is slow of speech, a shared commissioning problem stated differently.

column5: Aaron is appointed to meet Moses
column6: The commentary says Moses asks that his brother share the task so they can praise God; Exodus has God appoint Aaron, already on his way to meet Moses, as the brother who will speak with him.

column5: Aaron speaks while Moses is as God
column6: The commentary links a single messenger, his brother’s aid, and a divine mission; Exodus says Aaron will be Moses’ mouth and Moses will be as God to him, clarifying delegated speech without the Qur’anic stated purpose of praise.

column5: the name that answers is declared God
column6: The commentary contrasts the one true Lord with names humans assign to rivals; Elijah proposes a public test in which each side calls its god by name and the one who answers by fire is God.

column5: Baal’s name is called without an answer
column6: The commentary calls idolatrous names unsupported names; the prophets of Baal invoke their god from morning until noon, but no voice answers, giving that critique a concrete narrative scene.

column5: Elijah invokes YHWH’s name before Israel
column6: The commentary links praise of the name with a messenger’s public task; Elijah prays that the people will know YHWH is God and that he acted at YHWH’s word, making the name known through the sign.

column5: Israel confesses YHWH alone is God
column6: The commentary says divine lordship must not be distributed among rivals; after the fire, the people fall down and confess that YHWH is God, the scene’s explicit verdict on the competing names.

column5: Cain receives a protective mark
column6: The commentary develops a possible Arabic name-as-brand image but does not claim a Hebrew cognate; God marks Cain so others will recognize and spare him, adding protection to the mark’s identifying function.

column5: God gives Abram the name Abraham
column6: The commentary says a name raises and distinguishes its bearer; God renames Abram Abraham and explains the name by his future role as father of many nations, showing identity conferred by God.

column5: knowledge of YHWH compared with dawn and rain
column6: The commentary brings the first rain, green pasture, and the knowledge of God into one hearing; Hosea says let us know YHWH, whose coming is like dawn and like rain watering the land, a particularly close meeting of knowledge and agricultural renewal.

column5: YHWH is righteous, while the speaker rebelled
column6: The commentary says Jonah’s tasbih assigns perfection to God and wrongdoing to himself; Lamentations says YHWH is in the right while the speaker has rebelled, a direct ethical form of that reversal.

column5: stars and natural powers mistaken for gods
column6: The commentary distinguishes celestial motion from the Creator and rejects names placed on created things; Wisdom lists sun, moon, stars, and other natural powers as things people mistakenly treated as gods.

column5: creation’s greatness points to its Maker
column6: The commentary places the sky, stars, rain, and pasture under one sustaining Lord; Wisdom argues that the greatness and beauty of created things allow their Maker to be perceived, sharpening the distinction between sign and source.

column5: a good name rises above other crowns
column6: The commentary develops name as elevation and public distinction; this saying places the crown of a good name above kingship, priesthood, and Torah, giving Jewish ethical use to the image of a name raised above.

column5: the Lord’s Prayer recited three times each day
column6: The commentary joins tasbih to repeated prayer and embodied practice; the Didache instructs Christians to pray the Lord’s Prayer three times daily, turning its hallowing of the name into a regular liturgical act.

column5: Psalm 2’s royal “son” applied to Jesus
column6: The commentary rejects divine offspring; Hebrews quotes the royal son formula from Psalm 2 as speech about the Son, showing how Christian interpretation makes that Hebrew royal language christological.

column5: Israel called God’s firstborn son
column6: The commentary rejects God having a child; Exodus calls Israel God’s firstborn in a covenant demand to Pharaoh, showing that biblical son language can name a people’s relation to God rather than biological offspring.

column5: the lawless one exalts himself as God
column6: The commentary sets Pharaoh’s “I am your highest lord” against rightful divine sovereignty; Paul describes an end-time figure who exalts himself above every object of worship and proclaims himself God, a close later counter-image.

column5: the beast blasphemes God’s name
column6: The commentary says tasbih separates God from false claims about him; Revelation’s beast opens its mouth to blaspheme God’s name, giving a Christian apocalyptic image of the name’s profanation.

column5: seeing God’s face with his name on foreheads
column6: The commentary brings the divine face and a bodily name-mark into its reading; Revelation joins the two directly: the servants see God’s face and bear his name on their foreheads.

column5: one baptismal name over Father, Son, and Holy Spirit
column6: The commentary says different names belong to one possessor; Matthew gives baptism in the singular name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, a Christian formula that keeps unity while adding a distinct triune account.

column5: one king and one name over all the earth
column6: The commentary holds the highest Lord’s name apart from competing claims; Zechariah says YHWH will be king over all the earth and his name one, joining universal rule to exclusive naming.

column5: YHWH’s name and renown endure through generations
column6: The commentary contrasts the enduring highest name with fading life; this psalm says YHWH’s name and renown endure through all generations, extending the name’s permanence beyond an individual lifetime.

column5: YHWH’s name as a strong tower of refuge
column6: The commentary describes a name as a raised sign that protects and identifies its bearer; Proverbs says the name of YHWH is a strong tower into which the righteous run and are safe, making refuge part of the name’s force.
